passage: Tuesday, 1 am. Seventh rewrite of page one of the sociology essay. It was fine at nine, but then a word bothered me, then a comma, then the whole opening. Irawati, my roommate, mumbled from the bed, "It's good. Just submit." I said, "Not yet." The deadline is noon, I haven't started page two, and the statistics problem set is still unopened. If I submit something imperfect, they will see I'm not as good as they think. That is the real reason, I think. Not high standards. Fear. Okay. Ten minutes on page two, badly, no deleting. - Seema

qa.q: How many times had Seema rewritten page one?
qa.a: It was the seventh rewrite of page one.

qa.q: What is Seema really afraid of?
qa.a: That people will see the work is not as good as they think, so fear of criticism, not high standards, is behind the rewriting.

qa.q: What small step does Seema decide on?
qa.a: Ten minutes on page two, written badly, with no deleting.

qa.q: What does Irawati's mumbled comment suggest about how Irawati sees the page?
qa.a: Irawati finds it good already and is tired of waiting, seeing the rewrites as unnecessary.

grounding: Shows a student rewriting one page over and over, unable to submit anything flawed, while other work is neglected.

passage:
In their college library in Hyderabad, Disha looked across the table at Akash's screen. It was the same first page of his internship report she had seen on Monday. It was Thursday.
"How many times have you rewritten that?"
"Nine," Akash said. "The opening still sounds weak."
The report was due Friday. He had not started the data section. He had also skipped the Tuesday group meeting for another course, saying he needed to "get this right first."
Disha read the page. "Akash, this is good. Really."
He shook his head and deleted the second sentence again. Then, quietly: "If Professor Rao reads a bad first page, he'll think I'm not serious. He'll say something in front of everyone."
Disha put her hand over his keyboard. "He'll say something much worse if there's no data section." Akash stared at the screen, then saved the page as it was and opened a new file.

qa.q: How many times had Akash rewritten the first page?
qa.a: Nine.

qa.q: What was Akash afraid of?
qa.a: Akash was afraid of criticism, fearing Professor Rao would think he wasn't serious and say something in front of everyone.

qa.q: What did Disha do that helped Akash move on?
qa.a: Disha told him the page was good and pointed out the bigger risk of having no data section, so he saved it and moved on.

qa.q: How might the group from Tuesday's meeting see Akash's absence?
qa.a: They might feel let down or annoyed, not knowing that Akash's perfectionism was eating time from other work.

grounding: Shows a student who rewrites the same page again and again, hiding fear of criticism, while other work falls behind.

passage:
"Keerthana, it's two in the morning."
"I know. Just one more pass at the intro."
"How many passes is that?"
"Fourteen? I'm not counting."
Elizabeth sat up in bed. "The essay's due at nine. How much is left?"
"The whole middle part." Keerthana rubbed her eyes. "But if the intro isn't perfect, there's no point."
"Says who?"
"Dr Menon. She wrote 'weak opening' on my last one. In red. I can still see it."
"So you're scared she'll write it again."
Keerthana was quiet. "Maybe."
"Read me the intro."
Keerthana read it. Elizabeth said, "That's fine. It's clear. Leave it. Write the middle badly, then fix it at seven."
"Badly?"
"Badly and finished beats perfect and empty."
Keerthana laughed, a tired little laugh, and scrolled down. At 3:30 the middle was done. It wasn't her best writing. At nine she submitted it anyway, her hands a little shaky.

qa.q: What did Dr Menon write on Keerthana's last essay?
qa.a: She wrote 'weak opening' on my last one. In red.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she kept rewriting the intro?
qa.a: Keerthana was afraid of criticism, still stung by the red "weak opening" comment, and couldn't let the intro go.

qa.q: Which advice from Elizabeth worked, and why?
qa.a: "Write the middle badly, then fix it," because it let Keerthana stop polishing one part and actually finish.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel watching Keerthana at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Elizabeth is probably worried and a bit impatient, caring enough to sit up and help.

grounding: Illustrates a student who keeps rewriting one section, hiding fear of criticism, while the rest of the essay stays unwritten.

passage:
Last year I nearly failed my design course, and not because my work was bad. I'm Farhan, and I couldn't stop fixing it.
For the portfolio, I redid the cover page eleven times. Font, then spacing, then font again. Each version felt a little wrong. I told myself I just had high standards, and I was secretly proud of that.
Meanwhile, two other assignments slipped. I skipped my cousin's wedding weekend. I stopped sleeping properly.
Aparna, who shared my studio desk, finally said, "Farhan, what are you actually scared of?" I snapped at her. Then, walking home, I realised the answer: the jury. Being told, in front of everyone, that it wasn't good enough.
I submitted the next day with version eleven. The jury spent thirty seconds on the cover and twenty minutes on my ideas. They liked the ideas.
All those nights, and nobody even looked at the font.

qa.q: How many times did Farhan redo the cover page?
qa.a: I redid the cover page eleven times.

qa.q: What was Farhan really afraid of?
qa.a: Farhan was afraid of the jury, of being told in front of everyone that the work wasn't good enough.

qa.q: What could Farhan do differently on the next project?
qa.a: Farhan could set a limit on revisions, move on to the ideas and other assignments, and remember what the jury actually looks at.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when Farhan snapped?
qa.a: Aparna was probably hurt but concerned, since she had asked out of care about what was driving the rewrites.

grounding: Illustrates a student whose endless rewriting feels like high standards but hides fear of criticism and costs other important things.

passage:
Writing centre notes, 12 March. Student: Keerthana, second-year history.
Third session on the same essay introduction. She brought six printed versions of page one, each with tiny changes: "crucial" swapped for "vital", a comma moved, one sentence shifted to the end and then back. The body of the essay is still blank. The deadline is Friday.
When I asked what would happen if she sent a rough draft to her professor for comments, she went very still and said, "Then he'll know I'm not good at this." She also mentioned skipping badminton practice twice this week "to get the opening right".
What I did: set a timer for twenty-five minutes and asked her to write the next section badly on purpose, no deleting. She wrote a full page. Her hands were shaking at first.
Plan: meet Thursday. Page one is frozen until the body exists.
Damini, writing centre

qa.q: How many printed versions of page one did Keerthana bring?
qa.a: She brought six printed versions of page one.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana go very still when asked about sending a rough draft?
qa.a: She seemed afraid of being judged, believing a rough draft would show her professor that she is "not good at this".

qa.q: Which of Damini's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking Keerthana to write the next section badly on purpose, on a timer with no deleting, got a full page written and moved her past the frozen opening.

qa.q: How might Damini feel watching Keerthana's hands shake as she wrote?
qa.a: Damini was likely concerned at how much fear sat behind the rewriting, and encouraged that a full page came once deleting was off the table.

grounding: Shows a student rewriting one page over and over, unable to submit anything imperfect, while fear of criticism steals time.
